questions.question_text: How many members serve on the New Mexico Real Estate Commission?
questions.explanation: NMREC consists of 5 members appointed by the governor — 4 must be licensed brokers and 1 must be a public member who has never held a real estate license.

questions.question_text: Of the 5 NMREC members, how many must be licensed real estate brokers?
questions.explanation: NMREC has 5 members appointed by the governor: 4 must be licensed NM brokers and 1 must be a public member who has never held a license. This ensures both industry expertise and public representation.

questions.question_text: NMREC operates within which state department?
questions.explanation: NMREC is administratively attached to the Regulation and Licensing Department (NMSA 61-29-4.3), which houses New Mexico's professional licensing boards and commissions. The commission's five members are still appointed by the governor and exercise the powers granted by the Real Estate License Law.

questions.question_text: The governor appoints a retired school principal to NMREC who has never held a real estate license. This appointment fills which role?
distractors: An invalid appointment requiring a license
An alternate member without voting rights
questions.explanation: NMREC requires 1 of its 5 members to be a public member who has never been licensed as a real estate broker. The retired principal qualifies for this seat.

questions.question_text: Who appoints the members of the New Mexico Real Estate Commission?
questions.explanation: All 5 NMREC members are appointed by the governor of New Mexico. The Commission operates within the Regulation and Licensing Department but appointments come from the governor.

questions.question_text: Which action is NOT within NMREC's authority?
distractors: Imposing civil penalties for unlicensed real estate activity
Adopting rules for real estate practice
questions.explanation: NMREC licenses, adopts rules, investigates, disciplines, and may impose civil penalties for unlicensed activity (NMSA 61-29-17.2). Criminal prosecution belongs to the courts: the attorney general or district attorney prosecutes violations upon application of the commission (NMSA 61-29-17). The commission itself never prosecutes crimes.

questions.question_text: A brokerage keeps running misleading advertisements despite complaints. What is the License Law's mechanism for forcing the practice to stop?
questions.correct_answer: A court injunction sought by the attorney general or district attorney on the commission's application
distractors: A cease and desist order issued directly by NMREC
A criminal arrest warrant issued by the commission
An automatic license forfeiture without a hearing
questions.explanation: NMREC has no cease-and-desist authority. Under NMSA 61-29-17(B), the attorney general or district attorney may, upon application of the commission, sue in the state's name to enjoin violations or prosecute them. License discipline is also available through Uniform Licensing Act proceedings.

questions.question_text: NMREC's powers include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: NMREC oversees licensing, education approval, investigations, and trust account audits. Property tax rates are set by county taxing authorities, not the Commission.

questions.question_text: When NMREC needs to prosecute a license law violation, it works with which office?
distractors: The Office of the State Engineer
questions.explanation: Under NMSA 61-29-17(B), the attorney general — or the district attorney of the relevant judicial district — may, upon application of the commission, sue in the state's name to prosecute violations or enjoin unlawful practices. The AG's office also issues notices of contemplated action for disciplinary cases NMREC refers (16.61.36.9 NMAC).

questions.question_text: NMREC discovers a qualifying broker has been depositing client funds into a personal account. What is NMREC's FIRST enforcement step?
distractors: Refer to the county district attorney
questions.explanation: NMREC first investigates complaints and documents violations. An investigation may lead to no action, informal resolution, or a formal hearing — but investigation comes first.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum amount the NM Real Estate Recovery Fund will pay on a single judgment against a licensee?
questions.explanation: NMSA 61-29-23(A) caps recovery at $50,000 per judgment, regardless of how many people were aggrieved or parcels involved. A separate aggregate cap limits payouts for losses against any one licensee to $100,000 per calendar year. The per-judgment cap was raised from $10,000 effective July 1, 2021.

questions.question_text: Before filing a petition with NMREC for recovery from the fund, the aggrieved person must first:
distractors: Submit a written complaint to NMREC
questions.explanation: The Recovery Fund requires the claimant to first obtain a final judgment from a court of competent jurisdiction against the licensee, then file a verified petition with NMREC within 2 years.

questions.question_text: What may NMREC do to a broker's license after the Recovery Fund pays a claim based on that broker's conduct?
questions.correct_answer: Revoke, suspend, or refuse to renew it, at the commission's discretion
distractors: Nothing — the fund payment closes the matter
Revoke it automatically by operation of law
Issue a reprimand only, with no license action allowed
questions.explanation: NMSA 61-29-27 lets the commission revoke, suspend, or refuse to renew the license of a broker for whom the fund paid, and refuse to issue or renew any license until the fund is fully reimbursed. The action is discretionary, not automatic, and separate discipline under NMSA 61-29-12 remains available (61-29-29).

questions.question_text: A verified petition for recovery from the NM Recovery Fund must be filed within what time period after obtaining a court judgment?
questions.explanation: The aggrieved person must file a verified petition with NMREC within 2 years of obtaining a final court judgment. Missing this deadline forfeits the right to recover from the fund.

questions.question_text: A homebuyer obtains a $75,000 judgment against a broker for fraud. What is the most the Recovery Fund will pay on that judgment?
questions.explanation: The fund reimburses unpaid actual damages up to $50,000 per judgment (NMSA 61-29-23(A)). The remaining $25,000 stays collectible from the broker personally. A separate cap limits aggregate payouts for all claims against one licensee to $100,000 per calendar year — but it never raises the per-judgment limit.
